title: The Sharpe Pint: Custom Silicon, S&P 8,000, and the Art of the Ask

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you traded on Middle East peace rumours yesterday, hopefully you didn't bet the mortgage. Overnight drone strikes and some classic Trump commentary have put Brent crude back on the march, snapping the FTSE's eight-day winning streak. Meanwhile, Snowflake is dropping $6 billion on AWS's custom chips, Goldman is eyeing S&P 8,000, and we're looking at why your portfolio optimiser is probably lying to you. Grab a flat white, let's get into it.

content.text: Snowflake's $6 Billion Bet: AI is Shifting from GPUs to CPUs

Snowflake reported a stellar Q1 earnings beat, raising its FY27 product revenue forecast to $5.84 billion, and announced a massive five-year, $6 billion infrastructure commitment with Amazon Web Services (AWS). But the real story here is buried in the plumbing: Snowflake isn't buying more Nvidia GPUs; it's buying AWS's custom, Arm-based Graviton CPU chips. While GPUs are essential for training massive LLMs, the day-to-day running of AI agents, text-to-SQL queries, and data pipelines (inference) relies heavily on power-efficient CPUs. Amazon's custom silicon is undercutting Nvidia on price and winning the enterprise scale-out phase of AI.

For tech analysts and asset managers, this is proof that enterprise AI is moving from the 'experimentation' phase to the 'production' phase, where cost-efficiency is king. It also shows that the 'picks and shovels' trade is broadening out. Hyperscalers designing their own custom Arm-based silicon are capturing a massive share of the AI inference market, which is a structural tailwind for Arm Holdings and a long-term threat to Nvidia's absolute dominance.

Pub talk: Everyone's obsessed with Nvidia's GPU backlog, but the real margin battle in enterprise AI is shifting to custom CPUs. Snowflake committing $6 billion to AWS custom silicon proves that running AI agents at scale is a cost-efficiency game, not just a raw horsepower game.
AkzoNobel Rejects €12.5bn Consortium Breakup Bid

Dutch paint giant AkzoNobel rejected a joint cash proposal of €12.5 billion ($14.5 billion) from Japan's Nippon Paint and US-based Sherwin-Williams. The hostile bid proposed a breakup of AkzoNobel, where Nippon Paint would take the decorative and industrial coatings, and Sherwin-Williams would take automotive, marine, and powder coatings. AkzoNobel rejected the bid, choosing to stick with its existing $25 billion all-stock merger with Axalta Coating Systems (announced in late 2025). This highlights that while the 'megadeal' is back in 2026, hostile breakups and complex cross-border consortium bids face massive regulatory and board-level resistance.

For M&A bankers and arbitrageurs, this is a classic 'interloper' scenario. It shows that consolidation in the global chemicals and coatings space is reaching a boiling point. The rejection sent AkzoNobel's shares surging, as the market bets on either a sweetened bid or a bidding war.

Pub talk: The AkzoNobel rejection is a textbook case of why consortium break-up bids are incredibly hard to pull off. Boards hate the execution risk of splitting up assets between two buyers, especially when they already have an agreed merger of equals on the table like Akzo's deal with Axalta. But with Akzo's shares popping, the pressure is on.
Goldman Sachs Hikes S&P 500 Target to 8,000: It's an Earnings Story, Not a Bubble

Goldman Sachs chief US equity strategist Ben Snider raised the bank's year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,000 (from 7,600) and increased the 2026 EPS forecast to $340 (a 24% YoY jump). Unlike previous speculative rallies, Goldman's bull case is built on actual earnings growth rather than multiple expansion. The S&P 500's forward P/E multiple has actually declined 4% this year because earnings estimates are rising faster than stock prices. Crucially, Goldman notes that AI infrastructure beneficiaries will drive about half of this year's EPS growth.

For asset managers and quants, this is a green light for 'buy the dip' strategies. It creates a massive career risk for fund managers who are underweight US equities. If the index keeps climbing toward 8,000, active managers who sat on the sidelines will face severe underperformance.

Pub talk: Goldman's upgrade to 8,000 isn't just blind optimism; it's a fundamental earnings argument. When forward P/E multiples are actually falling because corporate profits are growing so fast, it's hard to argue we're in a classic speculative bubble. But it also means the market is incredibly concentrated—half of that growth is just the AI infrastructure trade.
US Banks Print Money, But Net Interest Margins Squeezed

The FDIC released its Q1 2026 Quarterly Banking Profile. US banks reported aggregate net income of $80.5 billion (up 3.6% QoQ) and a return on assets (ROA) of 1.26%. However, net interest margins (NIM) fell 8 basis points to 3.31% as asset yields fell faster than funding costs. While headline profitability looks robust, the underlying mechanics show that the 'higher-for-longer' rate environment is finally squeezing banks' margins. Earning asset yields are declining faster than the cost of deposits, and commercial real estate (CRE) and consumer portfolios continue to show elevated delinquency rates.

For credit analysts and bank equity investors, this is a warning sign. The deposit base grew (domestic deposits up 2.1%), but it was driven by uninsured domestic deposits, which are highly flighty. Additionally, the rise in 'All Other Loans' (often linked to non-bank financial institutions and private credit) is raising regulatory eyebrows.

Pub talk: US banks are printing money on paper, but the 8-basis-point drop in net interest margins shows the squeeze is on. If deposit costs stay sticky while loan yields soften, bank earnings are going to face a headwind in the second half. Plus, those CRE delinquencies aren't going away.
Hg Capital Commits $500m to Rightsline: PE's AI Playbook in Action

Leading transatlantic software investor Hg announced a $500 million strategic growth investment in Rightsline, a provider of rights and royalties management software for IP-intensive industries (like streaming, entertainment, and media). HgCapital Trust (HGT) will invest £11 million alongside other Hg funds. This is a classic mid-market private equity deal that shows how PE is deploying capital in 2026. Rightsline operates in a highly complex niche—tracking who owns what IP and who gets paid what royalties across global streaming platforms. Hg plans to use its dedicated AI product incubator to accelerate Rightsline's AI roadmap, automating complex royalty calculations.

For private equity and venture capital professionals, this deal highlights the ongoing trend of 'AI-enablement' in enterprise software. Rather than investing in raw AI models, PE is buying established SaaS businesses with sticky enterprise customers and using AI to drive operational efficiencies and product upgrades.

Pub talk: The Hg investment in Rightsline is a perfect example of how private equity is playing the AI boom. They aren't buying speculative AI startups; they're buying a boring, highly profitable SaaS business that manages complex IP royalties, and then using AI as an operational lever to supercharge the product.
Ofgem's 13% Energy Price Cap Hike: A Headache for the Bank of England

UK energy regulator Ofgem announced that the energy price cap will rise by 13% for the typical household from July 1 to September 30, 2026. This is a significant blow to UK consumers and a headache for the Bank of England. The hike is driven by persistent wholesale gas and electricity price volatility, largely linked to ongoing Middle East tensions. It means inflation risks remain sticky, which could delay further BoE rate cuts.

For macro traders and gilt investors, this sticky inflation print means the BoE's path to a lower terminal rate is fraught. Gilt yields are likely to face upward pressure, and consumer-discretionary stocks could see a pullback as household budgets are squeezed again.

Pub talk: Just when we thought inflation was under control, Ofgem's 13% price cap hike is going to keep the Bank of England on high alert. It's a classic reminder that the UK is still highly exposed to global energy shocks, and it makes any near-term rate cuts a much tougher sell for the MPC.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Geopolitical Ping-Pong: Peace Hopes and Drone Strikes

If you want a masterclass in how quickly geopolitical headlines can whip the market's tail, look no further than the last 24 hours. On Wednesday, Wall Street was in full 'peace dividend' mode. The S&P 500 nudged up to a fresh record of 7,520.36, and the Dow Jones climbed 0.4% to cross 50,644.28. The catalyst? A massive 4.6% plunge in Brent crude to $92.25 a barrel on whispers that the US and Iran were closing in on a ceasefire that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a month. Easing energy costs took the heat off inflation expectations, Treasury yields slid, and risk-on was the only game in town.

But as any seasoned City trader knows, trading on Middle East peace rumours is a dangerous game. Overnight, the cold water arrived. The US military launched 'defensive' strikes, shooting down four Iranian drones near the Strait of Hormuz and hitting a ground control station. President Trump then poured oil on the fire—literally—by dismissing reports of an imminent deal, asserting that Iran is 'negotiating on fumes'. Unsurprisingly, Brent crude bounced back over 2.5% to around $94.72, and the FTSE 100 snapped its eight-session winning streak, opening nearly 1% lower on Thursday morning to hover around 10,416.
The Sector Whiplash: From Airlines to Oil Majors

The sector rotation over the last two sessions has been pure whiplash. On Wednesday, the big winners were the fuel-guzzlers. Airlines and cruise lines soared on the prospect of sub-$90 US crude: United Airlines jumped 6.3%, Delta Air Lines rose 3% to an all-time high, and Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings gained 6.1%. Fast forward to Thursday morning in London, and those gains are being clawed back. Instead, it's the defensive oil majors like BP and Shell ticking up on the oil rebound, while mining heavyweights like Fresnillo (-3.9%) and Endeavour Mining (-3.8%) drag the FTSE down.

Meanwhile, the AI juggernaut remains completely insulated from geopolitical reality. Micron Technology gained another 3.6% on Wednesday, cementing its newly minted status as a $1 trillion company after a massive 19% surge earlier in the week. If you want a taste of how wild the enterprise tech spend still is, look at Snowflake. The software firm jumped 25% in after-hours trading after announcing a colossal $6 billion deal with Amazon Web Services to use AWS's new Graviton AI chips. When SaaS companies are signing multi-billion-dollar chip commitments, it's easy to see why Goldman Sachs just raised its year-end S&P 500 target to 8,000.
Under the Hood: The Cross-Asset Read

items: Rates: The US 10-year Treasury yield, which had eased to 4.48% on Wednesday as oil fell, ticked back up to 4.51% on Thursday morning as energy-led inflation fears crept back in. The German 10-year Bund yield similarly edged up to 3.01%.

FX: The US Dollar Index (DXY) clawed back some ground as safe-haven flows returned, though long-term concerns over the US fiscal deficit and potential tariff-driven volatility are keeping a lid on any massive breakout.

Equities: We are looking at a dual-speed market. On one hand, you have the AI infrastructure boom (semis, memory, cloud) which is entirely decoupled from the macro picture. On the other, you have a highly fragile consumer under pressure from high borrowing costs and sticky inflation.

content.text: The Pub Talk: How to Sound Smart at the Bar

If you're chatting with colleagues or clients today, the key talking point is the stark divergence between market levels and economic reality. The S&P 500 is sitting near record highs, and Goldman is forecasting $340 in EPS for 2026. Yet, underneath the hood, household balance sheets are showing serious cracks—credit card delinquencies are rising, and real wage growth is lagging. The market is essentially a levered bet on two things: that the AI capex cycle won't pop, and that geopolitical flare-ups in the Gulf remain 'contained'. If either of those assumptions falters, the downside from these valuations is substantial. It's a great time to be long quality and short complacency.

content.text: Operating Leverage: The Ultimate Margin Accelerator (and Decelerator)

If you want to understand why some stocks double on a minor revenue beat while others barely budge, you need to look at operating leverage. It’s one of the most powerful concepts in investing, yet it is frequently misunderstood or ignored until a company's earnings either explode to the upside or fall off a cliff.

In plain English, operating leverage is a measure of how sensitive a company’s operating income (EBIT) is to a change in its revenue. It is entirely driven by the mix of fixed versus variable costs in a business. If a company has high fixed costs and low variable costs, it has high operating leverage. Once those fixed costs are covered, almost every extra pound of revenue drops straight to the bottom line.
The Tale of Two Pubs
Let’s illustrate this with a simple example. Imagine two pubs in the City, both bringing in £1,000,000 in annual revenue and both currently making £200,000 in operating profit (EBIT).

items: The Alchemist (High Operating Leverage): This pub has high fixed costs (rent, expensive brewing equipment, salaried staff) of £600,000, and low variable costs (the actual cost of ingredients for the beer) of £200,000. Its gross margin is high, but its fixed cost base is heavy.

The Pint & Pony (Low Operating Leverage): This pub has low fixed costs (cheap rent, casual staff on zero-hours contracts) of £200,000, but high variable costs (it buys pre-packaged premium food and drinks to resell) of £600,000.

content.text: Now, let’s say a major financial conference comes to town, and both pubs experience a 10% increase in revenue to £1,100,000.

items: At The Alchemist, variable costs rise by 10% to £220,000. Fixed costs remain £600,000. Total costs are £820,000. New EBIT is £280,000. That is a massive 40% increase in operating profit from a 10% revenue bump! Its Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) is 4.0x.

At The Pint & Pony, variable costs rise by 10% to £660,000. Fixed costs remain £200,000. Total costs are £860,000. New EBIT is £240,000. That is only a 20% increase in operating profit. Its DOL is 2.0x.

content.text: The Alchemist's profits exploded because its cost structure is geared to reward volume. But remember, this is a double-edged sword. If revenue drops by 10% due to a tube strike, The Alchemist’s EBIT plummets by 40% to £120,000, while The Pint & Pony’s only drops by 20% to £160,000. Operating leverage magnifies both the glory and the pain.
Why It Matters in Asset Management

In public markets, identifying inflection points in companies with high operating leverage is where the real money is made. When a cyclical business (like a semiconductor fab, an airline, or a mining company) or a high-fixed-cost tech business (like a software-as-a-service provider) is about to cross its break-even point, consensus estimates are often way too conservative. Analysts model linear margin expansion, but the reality is non-linear. Conversely, when demand softens, these businesses burn cash at a terrifying rate, which is why they carry higher systematic risk (beta) even if they have zero debt on their balance sheet.
Common Beginner Mistakes

The classic mistake is confusing operating leverage with financial leverage. Financial leverage is about debt and interest payments (the capital structure). Operating leverage is about fixed operating costs (the business model). You can have a company with zero debt that is still incredibly risky and volatile because its operating leverage is through the roof.

Another mistake is assuming a high gross margin always equals high operating leverage. A software company might have a 90% gross margin, but if it has to constantly hire armies of enterprise sales reps (whose commissions and salaries are classified as SG&A, a fixed or semi-fixed cost), its operating leverage might be much lower than you think. You must look at the entire cost structure, not just cost of goods sold (COGS).
How to Ace This in an Interview
If an interviewer asks: 'How does a 10% increase in revenue affect a company's operating margin?', do not just say 'it goes up.' That’s a rookie answer. Instead, say:

It depends entirely on the company's operating leverage. If the company has a high proportion of fixed costs relative to variable costs—like a software business or a manufacturing plant—a 10% increase in revenue will lead to a disproportionately larger increase in EBIT, expanding the operating margin significantly. If it’s a low-operating-leverage business like a consultancy, where costs scale linearly with headcount, the margin expansion will be minimal. To give you a precise answer, I would need to look at the Degree of Operating Leverage, which is calculated as the percentage change in EBIT divided by the percentage change in revenue, or contribution margin divided by operating profit.
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

If you're chatting about a hyped-up stock with colleagues, you can drop this in: 'Everyone is valuing that new tech-enabled logistics player like a pure SaaS business because of its top-line growth. But if you look at their delivery partner payouts and warehouse leases, their cost base is almost entirely variable and semi-fixed. They don't have the operating leverage to justify a 15x sales multiple; their margins are never going to scale the way the market expects.'

content.text: The Problem with Markowitz (and why your optimiser is a liar)

Every junior quant learns Markowitz mean-variance optimization, and every senior quant knows it is a complete fantasy in production. If you feed a standard optimiser historical returns and covariances, it acts like a hyperactive toddler: it spots tiny, statistically insignificant differences in historical performance and leverages them to the moon. You end up with a portfolio that is 300% long on a random mid-cap stock and 200% short on a defensive utility, only for the whole thing to blow up the moment the market shifts. This is known as "error maximisation" or "estimation risk" in the trade.
Enter Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization (WDRO)

To stop your optimiser from hallucinating, we need robust optimization. But instead of just guessing some arbitrary bounds on our parameters, we can use Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization (WDRO). Instead of assuming our historical data distribution is the absolute truth, we draw a "ball" of alternative probability distributions around it. The radius of this ball (delta) is measured using the Wasserstein distance (also known as the Earth Mover's Distance—literally the minimum work needed to reshape one probability distribution into another). We then solve a minimax game: we find the portfolio weights that minimise our portfolio's variance under the worst-case distribution inside that Wasserstein ball.
The Magic of the Blanchet-Chen-Zhou Paper

Normally, solving an infinite-dimensional minimax problem over all possible probability distributions would require a supercomputer and several lifetimes. But a landmark paper by Jose Blanchet, Lin Chen, and Xun Yu Zhou (published in Management Science, 2022) pulled off a mathematical magic trick. They proved that if you define your uncertainty set using a Wasserstein ball, the terrifying minimax problem collapses into a simple, finite-dimensional convex optimization problem. Specifically, the distributionally robust portfolio is mathematically equivalent to minimising the standard empirical variance plus a regularisation penalty on the portfolio weights.

Why is this brilliant? For decades, practitioners have added heuristic penalties like Lasso (L1 norm) or Ridge (L2 norm) to their portfolio weights to keep them stable. It was a classic "it works in practice, but does it work in theory?" situation. The Blanchet et al. paper provides the rigorous proof: regularising your portfolio weights is mathematically identical to hedging against distributional uncertainty. If you use an L2 norm penalty, you are assuming a quadratic transport cost (meaning you are hedging against smooth, symmetric shifts in the market). If you use an L1 norm penalty, you are hedging against sparser, more concentrated shifts. Even better, the robust version of your expected return constraint automatically demands a higher empirical return "margin of safety" for assets where you hold concentrated weights.
Mini Technical Example (Python & CVXPY)

Here is how you can implement a Wasserstein robust mean-variance portfolio in Python using cvxpy. Notice how we do not need any complex simulation or adversarial training; the math simplifies it to a few lines of convex code.

import cvxpy as cp
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import sqrtm

# 1. Generate some dummy asset returns (5 assets, 100 days)
np.random.seed(42)
returns = np.random.normal(0.0005, 0.01, (100, 5))
mu_emp = np.mean(returns, axis=0)
Sigma_emp = np.cov(returns, rowvar=False)
Sigma_half = sqrtm(Sigma_emp).real  # Cholesky or symmetric square root

# 2. Set robust parameters
n_assets = 5
delta = 0.005  # Wasserstein radius (uncertainty budget)
target_return = 0.0008  # Desired portfolio return

# 3. Define CVXPY variables
phi = cp.Variable(n_assets)

# 4. Objective: Minimize empirical std dev + Wasserstein regularization
# This is the dual formulation of the worst-case variance minimization!
objective = cp.Minimize(cp.norm(Sigma_half @ phi, 2) + np.sqrt(delta) * cp.norm(phi, 2))

# 5. Constraints (including the robust expected return constraint)
constraints = [
    cp.sum(phi) == 1,
    phi >= 0,  # Long-only constraint
    mu_emp @ phi >= target_return + np.sqrt(delta) * cp.norm(phi, 2)
]

# 6. Solve the convex problem
prob = cp.Problem(objective, constraints)
prob.solve()

print("Robust Portfolio Weights:", np.round(phi.value, 4))
Over a Pint / Interview Angle

If you are interviewing for a buy-side quant role or chatting with a portfolio manager at the pub, this is a goldmine. You can explain that everyone knows Markowitz is an error maximiser, but instead of just slapping an arbitrary L2 penalty on the weights and calling it "shrinkage", we can use Wasserstein DRO. It proves that weight regularisation isn't just a heuristic hack—it's the exact dual of minimising risk under the worst-case distribution within a Wasserstein ball of uncertainty. What's really elegant is how the Wasserstein radius acts as a physical dial for your risk tolerance. A larger radius means you expect more structural drift or regime change in the market, which naturally forces the portfolio to diversify and demand a higher premium for concentrated bets.
Risks & Limitations

Before you go and replace your entire asset allocation pipeline, there are a few caveats. First, choosing the "right" Wasserstein radius is still a bit of an art. While the paper proposes a data-driven inference method (Robust Wasserstein Profile Inference), in practice, it relies on asymptotic assumptions that can break down in high dimensions (i.e., when you have more assets than historical data points). Second, the standard formulation assumes a symmetric transport cost. In reality, financial markets are highly asymmetric—we care a lot more about downside tail risk than upside surprises. If you want to handle asymmetric risk, you have to modify the transport cost function, which makes the dual optimization problem significantly more complex to solve.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Bento Box vs. The Stew: AQR on the 'Total Portfolio Approach'

If you have been paying attention to the big institutional allocators lately, you will have noticed a massive vibe shift. The California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS)—a cool $600 billion behemoth—is officially ditching its traditional Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) model on 1 July 2026. In its place, they are adopting the 'Total Portfolio Approach' (TPA). It is a trend pioneered by the likes of Canada’s CPPIB and the New Zealand Super Fund, but CalPERS’ move has turned it into the hottest talking point in asset management. To help us cut through the noise, AQR’s Portfolio Solutions Group recently dropped a brilliant, highly timely paper: 'Total Portfolio Approach: A Quant Lens' (published 19 May 2026).

Traditionally, asset allocation is like a bento box. You have rigid, siloed compartments: 60% equities, 40% bonds, maybe a little slot for private equity or real estate. Each slot has its own benchmark, and the team running it only cares about beating that specific index. TPA, on the other hand, is like a stew. There are no rigid buckets. Every investment—public or private, hedge fund or index tracker—must compete on a level playing field for its place in the portfolio, judged solely by its marginal contribution to the total fund’s risk and return.
Why This Paper Matters

While TPA sounds incredibly elegant in theory, the Financial Times recently dubbed it 'buzzy but fuzzy.' It is easy to write a glossy brochure about 'holistic investing,' but actually implementing it at scale is a different beast. AQR’s paper brings a characteristically sharp, quantitative, and slightly skeptical lens to the trend. It does not just cheerlead; it maps out the exact mathematical trade-offs, advantages, and—crucially—the hidden risks of throwing away your portfolio guardrails.
The Core Takeaways

items: Wrappers vs. Factors: Traditional SAA treats asset classes as separate islands. But a high-yield bond is just a corporate bond with a massive chunk of equity beta. TPA strips away the 'wrapper' (the asset class label) and looks at the 'ingredients' (underlying risk factors like equity beta, duration, liquidity, and credit). This eliminates the illusion of diversification.

The Governance Trap: Under SAA, if the real estate team underperforms, the board knows exactly who to blame. Under TPA, because everything is managed holistically, attribution is incredibly complex. AQR warns of 'heuristic collapse'—where boards get overwhelmed by the complexity of a unified portfolio and default to oversimplified, potentially dangerous decision-making rules.

Model Risk is the New Market Risk: If you do not have rigid asset class buckets, you are entirely reliant on your quantitative risk models to tell you your true exposures. If your model misestimates the correlation between your private equity holdings and public markets, you could end up taking on massive, unintended bets without realizing it.

Unlocking Capital Efficiency: On the positive side, removing rigid constraints allows allocators to use capital-efficient strategies like portable alpha, managed futures, and overlay derivatives. This lets them capture diversifying risk factors without tying up precious cash.

content.text: "The total portfolio approach to investing (TPA) has been aptly described as 'buzzy but fuzzy.' ... We identify a set of tangible advantages and a countervailing set of possible risks from removing traditional strategic asset allocation constraints or guardrails..."
How to Read It (and What to Skim)

If you are a quant PM or a risk specialist, by all means, dive into the four portfolio optimization demonstrations in the middle of the paper. For everyone else, skim the heavy matrix algebra. Instead, focus on the conceptual frameworks in Section 1 and Section 4, which lay out how to map different asset classes to their underlying risk factors. It is the best primer you will find on how modern, sophisticated allocators actually view risk.
The Pint-Sized Pitch: What to Say at Work
This is gold dust for interviews or client meetings. If someone brings up CalPERS or the trend toward TPA, you can sound like the smartest person in the room by saying:

"TPA is conceptually brilliant because it admits that asset class labels are just marketing wrappers—private equity is mostly just leveraged public equity, and high-yield is just a stock-bond hybrid. But as AQR points out, throwing away SAA guardrails is a massive double-edged sword. If your risk model is even slightly off on correlations, or if you hit a regime shift, you're essentially flying blind with a very expensive, very sophisticated model."
Our Take

TPA is the logical conclusion of factor investing, and for sophisticated shops with world-class risk systems, it is a massive upgrade. But for mid-sized pension funds or wealth managers jumping on the bandwagon because it sounds modern, it is highly dangerous. SAA buckets might be rigid and intellectually unsatisfying, but they act as vital guardrails against human error and model failure. Sometimes, a simple bento box is safer than a complex, over-engineered stew.

content.text: The Ben Franklin Effect: Stop sucking up, start asking for favours

We’ve all been there. You’re trying to win over a notoriously prickly Managing Director, or perhaps a cold institutional client who treats your emails like spam. The instinct is always to "add value" (read: suck up). You send them unsolicited market updates, offer to run extra analysis, or buy them expensive coffees. It rarely works. They either ignore you or treat you like a free resource.
There’s a better, highly counter-intuitive way to build rapport, and it’s called the Ben Franklin Effect.
The Concept

The Ben Franklin Effect is a psychological phenomenon where a person who has performed a favour for someone is more likely to do another favour for them than if they had received a favour from that person. It sounds completely backwards, but it’s rooted in cognitive dissonance. Our brains hate inconsistency. If we do a favour for someone we don't know well (or don't particularly like), our brain experiences a clash: "Why am I helping this person?" To resolve the tension, the brain rewrites the narrative: "I must help them because I actually quite like them and think they're promising."

This isn't just folk wisdom; it was proven in a classic 1969 study by psychologists Jon Jecker and David Landy. They found that participants who were asked by a researcher to return prize money as a personal favour rated that researcher significantly more favourably than those who were asked by a secretary or not asked at all.
How it works in the City

Imagine you’re trying to get a senior MD to sponsor your promotion. Instead of trying to impress them by working yourself to the bone on their pitch decks (which they expect anyway), you ask them for a small, low-stakes favour that appeals to their ego. Here are three ways to do it:

items: The "Advice" Ask: "I know you led the restructuring of [Company X] a few years ago. I'm looking at a similar capital structure now—do you have five minutes to tell me what the biggest hurdle was?"
The "Expertise" Ask: "I'm trying to get my head around how the new Basel rules might affect our leverage ratio. Who is the best person in the building to talk to about that?"
The "Recommendation" Ask: "I'm trying to improve my understanding of distressed debt. Is there a specific book or paper you'd recommend I read?"

content.text: Notice these aren't asking them to do your job for you. They are small, low-friction requests that allow the senior person to feel wise, helpful, and respected. By granting the favour, they subconsciously invest in your success.
How to use it (without being annoying)

The key to pulling this off without looking like a manipulative sociopath is keeping the request genuinely small and respectful of their time. Do not ask them to review a 50-slide deck. Do not ask for a favour that benefits you financially or directly (like "can you write my performance review?"). Ask for their perspective, their advice, or a quick introduction. And once they help you, make sure to follow up and let them know how their advice helped. That closes the loop and cements the relationship.
One line to remember
To win an ally in the office, stop trying to do them favours and start asking for small ones instead.
